title: Nontuberculous Mycobacteria: Runyon Groups, 30 °C Cultures and Species ID
summary: Sort nontuberculous mycobacteria into Runyon groups, know which skin pathogens need a 30 °C culture (fish tank granuloma), and choose probes, sequencing or MALDI-TOF to name the species, including why M. chimaera must be separated from the rest of the M. avium complex.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 59 Hit 9 (Runyon classification), Hit 11 (M. marinum, fish tank granuloma, 30 °C), Hit 18 (identification by probes, sequencing, MALDI-TOF), Exam Trap 4 (cutaneous specimens need a 30 °C set) and Exam Trap 6 (identify MAC to species after cardiac surgery: M. chimaera). Checked against Sharma 2020, Azadi 2018, Hashish 2018, Tsiolakkis 2023, Nookeu 2019, Alcolea-Medina 2019, Bagnarino 2022, Spagnolo 2024, Sommerstein 2018 and CDC HAN 00397 (read via a page-fetch tool). The CLSI-aligned ASM practical guidance (Forbes 2018, PMC5967691) was not readable: the PMC page returned a browser-verification page, the ASM site returned 403, and Europe PMC/NCBI gave only the abstract. Qualifications: sources define rapid growers as growth in under 7 days (reviewer: ≤7 days); the reviewer’s “1 in 100 to 1 in 1,000 surgeries” for M. chimaera is CDC’s estimate for patients in hospitals where at least one infection had been identified. Not taught: biochemical identification tests, scotochromogen pigment under light, M. gordonae pigment group, Xpert NTM speciation details, MAC in AIDS (Hit 10), M. leprae.

objectives: Assign a nontuberculous mycobacterium to a Runyon group from its pigment and growth rate.
Explain why skin specimens need an extra 30 °C culture and recognise fish tank granuloma.
Choose an identification method (probe, sequencing, MALDI-TOF) and explain why an invasive MAC isolate after cardiac surgery needs species-level identification.

scenes.title: Three isolates, three misses
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three mycobacterial cases. (1) Skin biopsy from nodules climbing the forearm of an aquarium owner, cultured only at 37 °C: no growth. (2) Sputum that is acid-fast smear positive but Xpert MTB/RIF negative. (3) A blood culture growing “M. avium complex” from a patient with a prosthetic heart valve placed two years ago. Question token: “What was missed, and what comes next?”

cues.text: Three mycobacterial cases. Skin nodules climb the forearm of an aquarium owner, and the biopsy, cultured only at thirty-seven degrees, grows nothing.
A sputum smear shows acid-fast bacilli, but the Xpert test for tuberculosis is negative.
And a blood culture grows Mycobacterium avium complex in a patient whose heart valve was replaced two years ago. What was missed, and what comes next?

props.label: What was missed, and what comes next?

scenes.title: Runyon groups: pigment and speed
scenes.altText: Schematic: four culture tubes. Runyon groups as summarised by Sharma 2020 and Azadi 2018. Slow growers (growth on subculture in 7 days or more): photochromogens make pigment on exposure to light (M. kansasii, M. marinum); scotochromogens make pigment when grown in the dark (M. scrofulaceum); nonchromogens grow unpigmented (M. avium complex). Rapid growers show growth in under 7 days on subculture (M. abscessus, M. fortuitum, M. chelonae).

cues.text: The Runyon scheme sorts nontuberculous mycobacteria by pigment and speed. Photochromogens make pigment only after exposure to light. Mycobacterium kansasii and Mycobacterium marinum are the classic examples.
Scotochromogens make pigment even when grown in the dark, such as Mycobacterium scrofulaceum.
Nonchromogens grow without pigment. The Mycobacterium avium complex belongs here.
The fourth group is defined by speed, not colour. Rapid growers show growth on subculture in under seven days: abscessus, fortuitum and chelonae.

scenes.title: Cool skin, cool incubator
scenes.altText: Temperature card (Sharma 2020): incubation of 36 ± 2 °C for slow growers and 28 ± 2 °C for rapid growers has been recommended; M. marinum and M. ulcerans need about 30 °C, M. xenopi 42–45 °C. M. haemophilum needs heme supplementation and 30–32 °C (Nookeu 2019). M. marinum card (Hashish 2018; Tsiolakkis 2023): optimal growth around 30–32 °C, inhibited at 37 °C; fish tank or aquarium granuloma after injuries during fish-tank or water exposure; spreads along lymphatics in a sporotrichoid pattern; chlorination of swimming pools has reduced exposure. Practice token: skin, bone and joint specimens also set at 30 °C.

cues.text: Most slow growers are incubated near thirty-six degrees. But several skin pathogens prefer it cooler: Mycobacterium marinum and Mycobacterium ulcerans grow best near thirty degrees, and Mycobacterium haemophilum needs thirty to thirty-two degrees plus added heme.
Rapid growers have also been recommended at about twenty-eight degrees. So skin specimens are commonly given a second set at thirty degrees, as well as the usual thirty-seven.
Mycobacterium marinum causes fish tank granuloma. It enters through small injuries during contact with aquariums or fish, and its growth is inhibited at thirty-seven degrees.
The lesion can spread up the lymphatics in a sporotrichoid chain of nodules. Chlorinated swimming pools have made the old name, swimming pool granuloma, rare.

scenes.title: Naming the species
scenes.altText: Identification cards. Probes (Azadi 2018; Sharma 2020): commercial nucleic acid hybridisation probes for M. tuberculosis complex, M. avium complex, M. kansasii and M. gordonae; cross-reactions can occur. Sequencing (Sharma 2020): rpoB, hsp65, 16S rRNA and the 16S–23S ITS; DNA sequencing is the most accepted method. MALDI-TOF (Sharma 2020; Alcolea-Medina 2019; Bagnarino 2022): fastest, but needs a mycobacteria-specific preparation (extraction protocols often add bead-beating or sonication; a simpler on-plate formic acid method has also been described) and has a limited database that cannot split species within MAC. M. chimaera card (Spagnolo 2024; Bagnarino 2022): a MAC species hard to separate from M. intracellulare — 16S genes differ by one base pair, a common line probe assay and standard MALDI-TOF libraries do not separate them. Hook answers.

cues.text: Once a mycobacterium grows, name the species. Commercial probes exist for the tuberculosis complex, the avium complex, kansasii and gordonae. A smear-positive, Xpert-negative specimen is an NTM suspect: culture it, then identify.

Gene sequencing of 16S ribosomal RNA, hsp65, rpoB or the spacer region is the most accepted method. MALDI-TOF is fastest, but mycobacteria need a special preparation method, and its database is limited.

Mycobacterium chimaera sits inside the avium complex and is hard to tell from Mycobacterium intracellulare: their 16S genes differ by a single base. Routine probes and standard libraries can call both just avium complex.
Back to the hook. Reculture the skin biopsy at thirty degrees. Identify the sputum isolate. And identify the valve patient’s isolate to species, because it could be chimaera.

lines: 2 AFB +, Xpert −: culture and identify NTM

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Skin specimens only at 37 °C” (✓ add a 30 °C set: M. marinum, M. ulcerans, M. haemophilum and rapid growers prefer it cooler); “Report MAC and stop” in a cardiac-surgery patient with an invasive isolate (✓ identify to species; M. chimaera is a MAC species linked to heater-cooler devices); “Smear positive, Xpert negative = contamination” (✓ suspect NTM; culture and identify).

cues.text: Trap one: skin specimens only at thirty-seven degrees. No: add a thirty-degree set, or marinum, ulcerans and haemophilum may never grow.
Trap two: report avium complex and stop, after cardiac surgery. No: identify an invasive isolate to species. It could be chimaera from a heater-cooler device.
Trap three: smear positive but Xpert negative means nothing is there. No: suspect a nontuberculous mycobacterium, culture it and identify it.

scenes.title: Flash, dark, plain, race
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Photo needs a FLASH, Scoto glows in the DARK, Non stays PLAIN, Rapids RACE in under a week — and cool skin needs a cool incubator.” Tokens: flash = photochromogen · dark = scotochromogen · plain = nonchromogen · race = rapid grower. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: photo needs a flash, scoto glows in the dark, non stays plain, and rapids race in under a week. Cool skin needs a cool incubator: thirty degrees.
Where it breaks: Runyon groups only sort; they never name the species. The seven-day boundary is worded differently between sources. And some species, like xenopi, prefer it hotter, not cooler.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Photo = light · scoto = dark · non = none · rapid < 7 days”, “Skin: add 30 °C · post-cardiac-surgery MAC: identify to species”.

cues.text: Sort nontuberculous mycobacteria by pigment and growth rate, add a thirty-degree culture for skin specimens, and identify invasive avium complex isolates after cardiac surgery to species, because Mycobacterium chimaera hides inside that complex.

props.label: Photo = light · scoto = dark · non = none · rapid < 7 days
Skin: add 30 °C · post-cardiac-surgery MAC: identify to species

explanation.what: Plain language: environmental mycobacteria are first sorted by whether they make yellow-orange pigment (only after light, even in the dark, or never) and by how fast they grow; then a molecular or mass-spectrometry test names the species. Some skin species only grow in a cooler incubator. Scientific terms: Runyon groups (photochromogen, scotochromogen, nonchromogen, rapid grower), slowly growing mycobacteria (SGM), rapidly growing mycobacteria (RGM), fish tank granuloma, sporotrichoid spread, nucleic acid hybridisation probe, targeted gene sequencing (16S rRNA, hsp65, rpoB, 16S–23S ITS), MALDI-TOF MS, M. avium complex (MAC), M. chimaera, heater-cooler device.
explanation.why: Species differ in where they live, which temperature they need and how they are treated. Cutaneous species such as M. marinum, M. ulcerans and M. haemophilum grow best near 30 °C and can be missed at 37 °C alone. M. chimaera, spread from contaminated heater-cooler devices during open-heart surgery, is a MAC species that routine tests often cannot separate from M. intracellulare.
explanation.measure: Pigment test after light exposure and in the dark; growth on subculture in under 7 days (rapid) vs 7 days or more (slow). Incubation: about 36 ± 2 °C for slow growers, 28 ± 2 °C for rapid growers, about 30 °C for M. marinum and M. ulcerans, 30–32 °C with heme for M. haemophilum. Identification: probes for MTBC, MAC, M. kansasii, M. gordonae; sequencing of 16S rRNA, hsp65, rpoB or ITS; MALDI-TOF after a mycobacteria-specific preparation (extraction protocols often add bead-beating or sonication; a simpler heat-killing plus on-plate formic acid method has also been described).
explanation.differs: Photochromogen (pigment only after light) vs scotochromogen (pigment in the dark); probe (few species, quick) vs sequencing (most accepted, broad) vs MALDI-TOF (fastest, database-limited, needs mycobacteria-specific preparation); MAC as a complex vs M. chimaera as a species.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the Runyon group from a pigment description, pick the incubation temperature for a skin biopsy from an aquarium owner, or choose the next step for an invasive MAC isolate after cardiac surgery.

mnemonic.text: Photo needs a FLASH, Scoto glows in the DARK, Non stays PLAIN, Rapids RACE in under a week — and cool skin needs a cool incubator (30 °C).
mnemonic.explanation: Links each Runyon group to its defining property and reminds you to add a 30 °C set for skin specimens.
mnemonic.limitation: Runyon groups only sort isolates and never name the species; the 7-day boundary is worded differently between sources; not every special species is cooler (M. xenopi prefers 42–45 °C).

analogyLimitations: Culture tubes and colonies are schematic.
Mnemonic is a sorting aid only; species identification needs probes, sequencing or MALDI-TOF.
takeaway: Sort nontuberculous mycobacteria by pigment and growth rate, add a thirty-degree culture for skin specimens, and identify invasive avium complex isolates after cardiac surgery to species, because Mycobacterium chimaera hides inside that complex.

questions.stem: A biopsy of nodules spreading up the forearm of an aquarium owner is sent for mycobacterial culture. Which incubation plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Incubate at 37 °C and also at about 30 °C
options.rationale: Correct. M. marinum grows best near 30–32 °C and is inhibited at 37 °C, so a second, cooler set is needed.
Incorrect. M. marinum may fail to grow at 37 °C, giving a false-negative culture.
Incorrect. That higher temperature suits M. xenopi, not the cutaneous species.

options.text: Skip culture because Xpert MTB/RIF will detect the organism
options.rationale: Incorrect. Xpert MTB/RIF targets M. tuberculosis complex; a nontuberculous species needs culture and identification.

questions.stem: A slowly growing mycobacterium forms buff colonies in the dark that turn yellow only after exposure to light. Which Runyon group is it?

options.rationale: Correct. Pigment produced only after light exposure defines a photochromogen, such as M. kansasii or M. marinum.
Incorrect. Scotochromogens are already pigmented when grown in the dark.
Incorrect. Nonchromogens, such as MAC, do not develop pigment.
Incorrect. The organism is slowly growing; rapid growers show growth in under 7 days on subculture.

questions.stem: Blood cultures from a patient who had a heart valve replaced two years ago grow a slowly growing nonchromogen that a probe calls M. avium complex. What should the laboratory do next?

options.text: Identify the isolate to species level with a method that can separate M. chimaera from M. intracellulare
options.rationale: Correct. M. chimaera is a MAC species linked to heater-cooler devices in cardiac surgery, and routine MAC-level tests often cannot separate it from M. intracellulare.

options.text: Report “M. avium complex” as the final identification
options.rationale: Incorrect. A complex-level report hides whether the isolate is M. chimaera.

options.text: Discard the isolate as an environmental contaminant
options.rationale: Incorrect. A MAC isolate from blood is an invasive specimen and must be worked up.

options.text: Re-incubate at 30 °C to confirm the identification
options.rationale: Incorrect. Temperature preference does not separate MAC species; molecular or validated mass-spectrometry methods are needed.

references.citation: Almoradie A. MEMORY LAB: The Memory-First Medical Laboratory Science Reviewer. 1st ed., v2.0. 2026. Chapter 59, TB and Other Mycobacteria (EPUB; no fixed page numbers).
references.usedFor: Curriculum source: scope and exam framing. Not used as verification.

references.citation: Sharma SK, Upadhyay V. Epidemiology, diagnosis & treatment of non-tuberculous mycobacterial diseases. Indian J Med Res. 2020;152(3):185-226. doi:10.4103/ijmr.ijmr_902_20
references.usedFor: Runyon groups with examples (Table I, after Runyon 1959); rapid growers <7 days and slow growers ≥7 days on subculture; incubation 36 ± 2 °C for SGM and 28 ± 2 °C for RGM, M. marinum and M. ulcerans 30 °C, M. xenopi 42–45 °C; probes (M. avium, M. intracellulare, M. gordonae, M. kansasii; cross-reactivity); sequencing of rpoB, hsp65, 16S rRNA, ITS as most accepted; MALDI-TOF fastest with limited database; AFB-positive, Xpert-negative specimens as NTM suspects for culture and identification.

references.citation: Azadi D, Motallebirad T, Ghaffari K, Shojaei H. Mycobacteriosis and Tuberculosis: Laboratory Diagnosis. Open Microbiol J. 2018;12:41-58. doi:10.2174/1874285801812010041
references.usedFor: Pigment groups (photochromogenic, scotochromogenic, non-chromogenic); slow vs rapid growth around 7 days; commercial probes for MTBC, MAC, M. kansasii and M. gordonae (acridinium-ester-labelled rRNA probes).

references.citation: Hashish E, Merwad A, Elgaml S, et al. Mycobacterium marinum infection in fish and man: epidemiology, pathophysiology and management; a review. Vet Q. 2018;38(1):35-46. doi:10.1080/01652176.2018.1447171
references.usedFor: M. marinum photochromogenic Runyon group I; optimal growth at 30 °C, hardly at 37 °C; fish tank granuloma; sporotrichoid spread; chlorination reducing swimming-pool exposure.

references.citation: Tsiolakkis G, Liontos A, Filippas-Ntekouan S, et al. Mycobacterium marinum: A Case-Based Narrative Review of Diagnosis and Management. Microorganisms. 2023;11(7):1799. doi:10.3390/microorganisms11071799
references.usedFor: M. marinum grows best at 30–32 °C, inhibited at 37 °C, limited above 33 °C; photochromogen; risk factors include fish tank or aquarium contact and injuries; lymphatic sporotrichoid spread; “swimming pool granuloma” obsolete because of chlorination.

references.citation: Nookeu P, Angkasekwinai N, Foongladda S, Phoompoung P. Clinical Characteristics and Treatment Outcomes for Patients Infected with Mycobacterium haemophilum. Emerg Infect Dis. 2019;25(9):1648-1652. doi:10.3201/eid2509.190430
references.usedFor: M. haemophilum needs heme-supplemented medium and 30–32 °C; skin and soft tissue the most common site; study laboratory also incubated skin, bone and joint specimens at 30 °C.

references.citation: Alcolea-Medina A, Fernandez MTC, Montiel N, et al. An improved simple method for the identification of Mycobacteria by MALDI-TOF MS (Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption- Ionization mass spectrometry). Sci Rep. 2019;9(1):20216. doi:10.1038/s41598-019-56604-7
references.usedFor: MALDI-TOF identification of mycobacteria has used a dedicated extraction method (Bruker MycoEX), modified with cell disruption (sonication or bead-beating) to liberate protein; the paper itself describes a simpler method (heat killing, then neat formic acid on the target plate), so a bead-beating step is not always required.

references.citation: Bagnarino J, Barbarini D, Russello G, et al. Mycobacterium chimaera Identification Using MALDI-TOF MS Technology: A Practical Approach for the Clinical Microbiology Laboratories. Microorganisms. 2022;10(6):1184. doi:10.3390/microorganisms10061184
references.usedFor: M. chimaera and M. intracellulare are hard to separate; GenoType CM/AS cannot differentiate them; currently available MALDI-TOF libraries cannot without additional spectral analysis.

references.citation: Spagnolo AM, De Giglio O, Caggiano G, et al. The Spread of Mycobacterium chimaera from Heater-Cooler Units and Infection Risk in Heart Surgery: Lessons from the Global Outbreak? Pathogens. 2024;13(9):781. doi:10.3390/pathogens13090781
references.usedFor: M. chimaera is a MAC species once misidentified as M. intracellulare; MAC species-level differentiation is critical; 16S genes differ by one base pair; ITS sequencing suggested; symptoms on average 15–17 months after surgery, range 6 weeks to more than 5 years; case definition requiring M. chimaera identified by DNA sequencing from an invasive sample.

references.citation: Sommerstein R, Hasse B, Marschall J, et al. Global Health Estimate of Invasive Mycobacterium chimaera Infections Associated with Heater-Cooler Devices in Cardiac Surgery. Emerg Infect Dis. 2018;24(3):576-578. doi:10.3201/eid2403.171554
references.usedFor: Heater-cooler device association with invasive M. chimaera after cardiac surgery; long incubation (median 17 months, range 3–72 months).

references.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. CDC Advises Hospitals to Alert Patients at Risk from Contaminated Heater-Cooler Devices Used during Cardiac Surgery. Health Alert Network, CDCHAN-00397. October 13, 2016.
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool. Patients who had open-heart surgery with Stöckert 3T heater-cooler devices at risk; in hospitals where at least one infection had been identified, risk between about 1 in 100 and 1 in 1,000 patients; symptoms can take months to appear. Does not itself state a species-identification rule.

claims.text: Runyon groups: photochromogens (pigment after light; M. kansasii, M. marinum), scotochromogens (pigment in dark; M. scrofulaceum), nonchromogens (MAC), rapid growers (<7 days on subculture; M. abscessus, M. fortuitum, M. chelonae).

Incubation temperatures: about 36 °C slow growers, 28 °C rapid growers, 30 °C M. marinum and M. ulcerans, 30–32 °C plus heme M. haemophilum, 42–45 °C M. xenopi; skin specimens need an extra 30 °C set.
M. marinum: fish tank granuloma after injury with aquarium or fish exposure; growth inhibited at 37 °C; sporotrichoid lymphatic spread; chlorination reduced swimming-pool cases.

Identification: probes for MTBC, MAC, M. kansasii, M. gordonae; sequencing of 16S rRNA, hsp65, rpoB, ITS most accepted; MALDI-TOF fastest but needs a mycobacteria-specific preparation and has database limits (cannot split species within MAC); AFB-positive, Xpert-negative specimen is an NTM suspect for culture and identification.

M. chimaera is a MAC species linked to heater-cooler devices in cardiac surgery, hard to separate from M. intracellulare by routine tests, with symptoms months to years after surgery; invasive MAC after cardiac surgery should be identified to species.
Per-patient M. chimaera infection risk of about 1 in 100 to 1 in 1,000.
claims.note: Not taught in the lesson. CDC gives this figure only for patients in hospitals where at least one infection had been identified; the reviewer states it per surgery without that qualifier (register flag rv-chimaera-risk-context).

claims.text: Scotochromogens are pigmented in both dark and light; M. gordonae group assignment.
claims.note: Not taught; the sources read describe scotochromogens only as producing pigment in the dark.

claims.text: Scenario invented; cultures and colonies schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 59 Hit 9 defines rapid growers as growth in ≤7 days; Sharma 2020 and Azadi 2018 define them as growth in under 7 days (slow growers ≥7 days). The lesson uses “under 7 days” and notes that wording differs (register flag rv-rapid-grower-boundary).

Ch. 59 Exam Trap 6 gives an M. chimaera infection risk of “~1 in 100 to 1 in 1,000 surgeries”; CDC HAN 00397 gives that range per patient only in hospitals where at least one infection had been identified, after open-heart surgery with Stöckert 3T heater-cooler devices. The lesson does not teach the figure (register flag rv-chimaera-risk-context).

morphology.note: No photographs of colonies or lesions; groups and methods shown as cards.
